extracted.intended_audience: MIT researchers, inventors, students, staff, visitors, and prospective licensees
extracted.subtask_description: FAQ guidance from MIT's Technology Licensing Office about invention disclosure, IPIA/ownership, public disclosure timing, licensing types, payments, and administrative procedures related to MIT-owned intellectual property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of tangible property / research tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically, tangible property or research tools are materials such as antibodies, vectors, plasmids, cell lines, mice, and other materials used as “tools” in the research process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research tools do not necessarily need to be protected by patents in order to be licensed to commercial third parties and generate revenue for your laboratory. Other research tools (such as new separation processes) may need to be patented so that a company will invest in the engineering development to make the process broadly useful. If you have tangible property that you believe to be valuable, the TLO will work with you to develop the appropriate protection, licensing, and distribution strategy. The TLO will also help you distribute research materials at zero or minimal charge to other academic collaborators while preserving the materials’ commercial potential. Download the Research@MIT app to disclose research tools or tangible property.

rubrics_metrics.name: When/how to disclose before public disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete an invention disclosure whenever you feel you have discovered something unique with possible commercial value, and do so well before presenting the discovery through publications, poster sessions, conferences, press releases, or other communications including websites or social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing or sharing these ideas may also constitute a public disclosure, as does selling or offering for sale a prototype of the invention. Once publicly disclosed, an invention may have restricted or minimal potential for patent protection. If you have already submitted a disclosure, inform the TLO of the deadline for your publication/poster or presentation to determine whether a patent filing is first necessary. Publishing in advance of a patent application being filed may result in loss of patent rights. If possible, disclose your invention several months before it is to be publicly disclosed to ensure it may be properly protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public disclosure effects on patent rights and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Dates of public disclosure are important because foreign patent rights are lost once an invention has been publicly disclosed; in the US an inventor has one year from the date of public disclosure to file a patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of March 16, 2013 the US switched to a 'first-inventor-to-file' system. Public disclosure includes oral presentation at a public meeting, written disclosure, or offering it for sale. It is best to file before the public disclosure; once the one-year US grace period has passed the invention cannot be patented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of contract/grant information to TLO
rubrics_metrics.description: Under federal law, MIT is required to report inventions created under federally funded research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Institute decides not to take title to such an invention, the invention is returned to the Government under its primary ownership rights; if the Government doesn't wish to pursue it, it may be assigned back to the inventors. Non-government sponsors may also have intellectual property license rights included in sponsored research agreements with which MIT must comply. Provide contract/grant information so TLO can meet reporting and sponsorship obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting inventive contributions of non-MIT inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: All contributors to the ideas leading to an invention should be mentioned in your disclosure, even if they are not MIT employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The TLO, along with legal counsel, will determine the rights of such persons and their associated institutions. It is prudent to discuss collaborations (preferably before they begin) with the TLO to understand the implications for any arising inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of research sponsors vary by contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Rights granted to research sponsors vary according to the contract put in place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For more information reach out to OSATT. Sponsors' contracts may grant rights that affect assignment and licensing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPIA requirement by law (Bayh-Dole related)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal funding regulations (35 US Code Chapter 18 § 200-212, the Bayh-Dole Act) specifically require federally funded research entities to have, on file for every person participating in a research program, an agreement to assign ownership of certain intellectual property to the research entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following the federal government, industrial and foundation research sponsors require MIT to own and control certain intellectual property as a condition of receipt of research funds. Failure to have an individual’s signed IPIA on file puts MIT at risk of default of such regulations and obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of MIT Intellectual Property Policy and IPIA
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the Intellectual Property Policy is to encourage the free exchange of intellectual property by putting the responsibility for its protection into the hands of the Institute and not the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mission of MIT’s TLO is to protect (e.g., via filing patents) and license MIT-owned intellectual property to third parties. By signing the IPIA and transferring ownership of intellectual property to MIT, you place that IP into MIT’s hands to preserve it for your own further research and development while fulfilling the Institute’s mission and obligations to third party funders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to the IPIA requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: There are a few very rare exceptions to the IPIA requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions include some federal employees, participants in Knights Fellows Program, HHMI employees, and Whitehead appointees. HHMI employees are obligated to sign the IPIA only if they remain at MIT after their HHMI appointment has concluded. Otherwise the requirement applies to all persons having an opportunity to participate in research at the Institute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visitors/research affiliates and employer obligations for IPIA
rubrics_metrics.description: MIT expects its visitors and research affiliates to expressly confirm that they have no obligations to their employers that would conflict with the obligations codified by the IPIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The TLO will work with the research and commercial institutions that support visitors and affiliates to give them the opportunity to work and learn at MIT. If an employer has questions about the IPIA they can contact tlo-ipia@mit.edu.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to re-sign the IPIA after status changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-signing the IPIA depends on the type of status/appointment change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples requiring re-signing include employee to visitor, visitor to employee, undergraduate to graduate student/employee/visitor. Contact tlo-ipia@mit.edu with questions about whether you need to re-sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling conflicting IP or confidentiality agreements with other institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have signed IP or confidentiality agreements at another institution as well as the IPIA at MIT you should connect with your TLO officer to discuss specifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some instances, the IP you generate may need to be jointly assigned to MIT and the other institution, which may affect assignment commitments MIT has made to its research sponsors. Your TLO officer can navigate your specific situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: NDAs / outside consulting and conflict with MIT obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have been asked to sign an NDA for a for-profit company you should discuss these obligations with the Institute Conflict of Interest Officer and review MIT’s conflict of interest policies concerning outside professional activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is your responsibility to ensure the terms of any consulting agreement do not conflict with your commitments to MIT, including IP assignment obligations. You may consider appending the consulting rider to any agreement you sign; see the OGC website for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: TLO scope re: licensing technology from other entities
rubrics_metrics.description: TLO does not help with outside licensing of third-party technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incoming data use requests are managed by OSATT via the NDA/DUA (Hermes) Portal. Incoming material transfer agreements are managed by OSATT (TLO assists with Tangible Property Licensing/formerly outgoing MTAs). Other incoming IP license requests for research purposes that are fee-free (e.g., software licenses) should be directed to the Office of General Counsel (mitogc@mit.edu). Incoming software licenses that require payment should be directed to the contracts group in the Office of the Vice President of Finance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research use only license vs commercial license
rubrics_metrics.description: A research use license permits the licensee to use the relevant IP only for research purposes and not to practice the IP in a way that results in a commercially sold product or service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commercial license permits, and oftentimes requires, that the relevant IP be practiced in a way that leads to products and/or services that are sold commercially. Open source licenses (e.g., MIT/BSD) permit commercial use without compensation; if intent is to release software in an open access manner without granting commercial rights, the TLO suggests using a non-commercial, research use only license rather than an open source license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright notice for MIT-owned works
rubrics_metrics.description: What type of notice should be included on all MIT-owned copyrightable works?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use: “Copyright © [Year] MASSACHUSETTS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY. All rights reserved.” The date should be the year in which the copyrightable work is first published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting trademark registration
rubrics_metrics.description: I want MIT to register a trademark for some piece of technology or research or to identify a program or project within a DLC; what should I do?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact tlo-trademarks@mit.edu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal use of names or logos — pre-check actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before informally using a certain name or logo to describe technology, research or a program/project, review trademark issues and consult with TLO/OGC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the Office of General Counsel's article on trademark issues and consider speaking with the TLO at tlo-trademarks@mit.edu and/or the OGC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee payments — contact information and invoicing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whom to contact with invoice/billing questions related to licensing MIT IP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact the TLO Financial Manager, MIT Technology Licensing Office, 255 Main Street NE18-501 Cambridge, MA 02142-1493. Email: tlo-fina@mit.edu.

rubrics_metrics.name: MIT tax ID and request for taxpayer forms
rubrics_metrics.description: What is MIT's tax ID # and how to request taxpayer forms?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MIT tax ID # is 04-2103594. Email tlo-fina@mit.edu if you need a copy of the taxpayer ID form (Form W-9) or the sales tax-exempt purchaser certificate (Form ST-5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepted forms of payment for licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: TLO is able to accept the following forms of payment from those wishing to license MIT technology: credit card, wire/ACH transfers, check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit card payments have a $15,000 limit. Wire and ACH transfers must be sent in US dollars with a confirmation email to tlo-invoice@mit.edu. Checks made out to 'MIT Technology Licensing Office'. Wire/ACH bank details and comments (e.g., 'MIT Incoming Wire', routing/account numbers, SWIFT) provided on request to facilitate payment; include MIT TLO and Invoice # or Agreement # in the comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty reporting requirement even with zero sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Do I still need to submit MIT a royalty report even though we have had no commercial sales?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yes. Royalty reports are due regardless of whether there have been commercial sales. Zero-dollar royalty reports are easiest sent via email to tlo-royaltyreport@mit.edu.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to connect with TLO/licensing officer
rubrics_metrics.description: Connect with the TLO team or your licensing officer to explore opportunities and gain tailored guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact links provided on the TLO site to connect with your licensing officer for tailored guidance.
